results.title: Norwegian authorities reportedly detained two Chinese cargo ships on October 14.
results.description:
Norwegian authorities reportedly detained two Chinese cargo ships on October 14. One of them, Ya Qing Hai Yang, is under sanctions for its links to Arctic LNG 2, a Russian natural gas project on the Gydan Peninsula.

According to Starboard Maritime Intelligence, the vessel was spotted near the Norwegian border in early October. Flying the Guatemalan flag, it had sailed from Hong Kong via the Northern Sea Route, making several stops in the Far East.

In 2024, Ya Qing Hai Yang transported power generation modules from China to Russia's Utrenny port, which serves the Arctic LNG 2 project. The shipment led to the vessel being sanctioned by the U.S., EU, and Switzerland.

The second vessel, Jian Yang Cheng He, is not under sanctions, and no links to Russian projects have been reported.

According to the Norwegian Coast Guard, the vessels had sought shelter from a storm near Andøya Island in northern Norway. Coast Guard personnel conducted an inspection.

Both vessels reportedly remain off the Norwegian coast.

results.title: 🇳🇴 🇷🇺 As Washington explores sanctions relief for shadow-fleet oil tankers, Norway has inspected two Chinese heavy-lift cargo vessels, inclu
results.description:
🇳🇴 🇷🇺 As Washington explores sanctions relief for shadow-fleet oil tankers, Norway has inspected two Chinese heavy-lift cargo vessels, including one sanctioned for supporting Russia's Arctic LNG 2 project.

The Norwegian Coast Guard boarded the vessels near Andøya in northern Norway after they sought shelter from severe weather. One of them, Ya Qing Hai Yang, formerly Ocean 28, is under sanctions for transporting power-generation modules to Arctic LNG 2, Russia's flagship Arctic gas project targeted by Western restrictions.

The second vessel, Jian Yang Cheng He, is not sanctioned and has no publicly established connection to Russian energy projects. Norwegian authorities have not announced violations arising from either inspection.

The boarding took place around October 14, but the incident has drawn renewed attention as Washington outlines a different approach to vessels previously excluded from international trade.

According to Bloomberg, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright says the Trump administration is working on a mechanism that would allow investors to acquire sanctioned shadow-fleet tankers, refurbish them and return them to legitimate commercial service transporting non-sanctioned oil. Wright argues that rehabilitating these vessels could increase global shipping capacity and help stabilize energy markets. The administration says the process would not authorize continued transportation of sanctioned Russian or Iranian cargo.

The two developments concern different categories of ships. Norway inspected heavy-lift cargo vessels, one linked to sanctioned Russian energy infrastructure, while Washington's proposal concerns oil tankers that could be removed from sanctions under specified conditions.

Nevertheless, they illustrate an important question facing Western sanctions policy: how to prevent restricted vessels and their owners from continuing to support Russia's energy sector while permitting some previously sanctioned maritime assets to return to legitimate trade.

Who owns the vessels, who receives the proceeds from their sale, and whether sanctioned Russian interests retain any economic benefit will determine how meaningful the safeguards are.

For Moscow, maritime logistics remain essential to maintaining energy exports and financing the war in Ukraine. For Western governments, the challenge is enforcing restrictions without creating new opportunities for sanctions evasion.

results.title: 🇨🇳‼️ Kremlin has increased the gas discount for China to 56%.
results.description:
🇨🇳‼️ Kremlin has increased the gas discount for China to 56%.

The discount on Russian gas purchased by China via the Power of Siberia pipeline, launched seven years ago, will reach an unprecedented level this year, according to budget law materials published in the State Duma database.

Gazprom's average annual price for the Chinese market will be $247.9 per thousand cubic meters. Meanwhile, the company's other customers abroad will pay $562. This brings the discount to $315 per thousand cubic meters, or 56%.

Compared to last year, the discount for China will increase by 15%: then, China purchased gas for $240.3 per thousand cubic meters, compared to $406.5 from Gazprom's other customers abroad (a 41% discount).

Next year, according to budget documents, the Kremlin will continue to sell gas to Beijing at practically half price: $251.3 per thousand cubic meters, 46% lower than other foreign supplies ($450).

For 2028, the Ministry of Economic Development is projecting a reduction in discounts to 32% ($247.8 versus $361.9), and for 2029, to 24% ($246.4 versus $323.2).
